claims.text: The starting alloy is equal-atomic NbMoTaW.
Untreated NbMoTaW has a homogeneous single-phase BCC structure.
NbMoTaW has very poor room-temperature ductility.
NbMoTaW retains high mechanical strength at 1600 °C.
NbMoTaW has theoretically predicted irradiation resistance.
High-temperature solutionizing followed by rapid quenching will establish or preserve a homogeneous single-phase BCC NbMoTaW matrix.
Moderate-temperature aging of quenched NbMoTaW will nucleate finely dispersed nanoscale secondary precipitates.
The aging-induced precipitates may have a B2-type structure.
The precipitates will be uniformly dispersed within the BCC matrix.
Nanoscale precipitates can facilitate room-temperature dislocation motion in NbMoTaW.
The precipitates will act as barriers that promote dislocation bypass.
The precipitates may act as stress concentrators that enhance room-temperature plastic deformation.
Small precipitates with coherent matrix interfaces will minimally interfere with the dislocation mechanisms responsible for high-temperature strength.
The precipitates are not expected to create significant new defect sinks that compromise irradiation resistance.
The two-step heat treatment will significantly increase room-temperature ductility or fracture strain relative to untreated NbMoTaW.
Heat-treated NbMoTaW will retain yield strength at 1600 °C similar to that of untreated NbMoTaW.
Heat-treated NbMoTaW will show no significant degradation in irradiation resistance relative to untreated NbMoTaW.
Preserving high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance requires the precipitate volume fraction to remain low and the precipitate size to remain nanoscale.
Aging temperature and duration must avoid unwanted phase transformations while producing precipitates beneficial to room-temperature ductility.
